newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German employers reject hours cut for jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German employers reject hours cut for jobs.

text.p: German labour leaders on Wednesday defended a two-day jobs summit against accusations that it was a "talking shop", but employers immediately rejected a union proposal to create jobs by shortening the working week.

On the defensive against critics, Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy chief of the German trade union federation DGB, warned not to expect too much from the union-organised jobs meeting, which falls at a time when record unemployment has heightened public concern.
"We should not push expectations too high. There are no patent cures on offer," Engelen-Kefer told German radio.

Klaus Zwickel, head of the vast metal and engineering union IG Metall, called for a punctual start to European economic and monetary union (EMU) in a speech to the congress, adding the single currency would create a sound economic environment for job creation.
He also attacked Chancellor Helmut Kohl for failing to reduce the jobless queues that have reached record levels above 4.5 million people in recent months.

"Helmut Kohl wanted to go down in history as the chancellor of national unification. Helmut Kohl will leave the political stage as the chancellor of social division," Zwickel said on the second day of the conference.

But the illusory nature of quick fixes to Germany's unemployment problem became clear as a concrete proposal to the meeting from Zwickel, urging further cuts in working hours, was immediately rejected by employers.

Zwickel said that, in a first step, a 35-hour week already adopted in the engineering sector should be implemented throughout industry in a bid to halve Germany's unemployment by 2000, the stated goal of the Bonn government.
"Together with the reduction in overtime and the increase in part-time work a 35-hour working week must be put through in all industry sectors," Zwickel said.
For his own sector, Zwickel proposed a shift to a 32-hour week with some workers working only a four-day week, adding that this would entail some reduction in pay.

IG Metall pushed through a reduction in the working week to 35 hours from 40 amid great triumph in the early 1990s, negotiating for total wages to remain unchanged despite the smaller number of hours worked by the individual employee.
But the proposal of a further cut in working time, even with some flexibity on the pay side, was immediately rejected by the engineering employers' association Gesamtmetall.
"A general 32-hour work-week anchored in pay contracts is rejected in the strongest terms, completely independently of the level of pay compensation offered," the employers said.

Commenting on the proposal, Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said he thought politicians had no role to play in the debate over wages and working hours in Germany.
"On the matter of working hours, union and employer wage negotiators are better placed to solve the conflict than politicians," Schaeuble said.
His comments appeared to undermine the chances for a renewed attempt at last year's failed "alliance for jobs" pact between government, unions and employers.
The pact sought to link wage moderation by unions to job creation measures by employers and the government.
In the absence of domestic impetus for the jobs market, Zwickel called for a timely start to a European single currency which he said should embrace as many currencies as possible.
In order to join the currency union, nations must meet a set of strict entry criteria, including low budget deficits, government debt and stable exchange rates.
The currency union is scheduled to be launched on January 1, 1999 with as many nations as meet these criteria.
German policy-makers have generally favoured a very strict interpretation of the entry criteria, arguing that this would be necessary to ensure the stability of the new currency, euro.
He added that such policies ran the risk of excluding founding members of European Union from EMU.

Zwickel said the Maastricht Treaty governing entry to EMU did not include any one-sided determination for binding fiscal convergence criteria, but added that it did include " a clear determination of labour market goals".
